profiles.meeting_scenario: A tertiary-care hospital toxicology service is holding a troubleshooting meeting after several recent overdose case reports drafted by the ICU-pharmacy collaboration were flagged by the journal's internal review board for using the Naranjo Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Scale to argue that seizures and hypotension were caused by treatments given during resuscitation. The immediate context is that the team needs to diagnose why this language keeps appearing in manuscripts and case conference summaries despite prior education. The agenda is to review one representative mixed-overdose case, identify where the causal-framing process is going wrong, and decide on a practical fix for future write-ups and review workflows. The expected outcome is agreement on a revised documentation approach and a screening step before cases are submitted or presented.

members.name: Dr. Elena Varga
members.expertise: Bedside toxicology consultation, causality assessment in poisoning, case report authorship
members.background: Attending physician at a regional poison center embedded in an academic hospital; trained in emergency medicine and medical toxicology; frequently reviews overdose manuscripts and teaches fellows how to distinguish toxic effects from treatment-related complications.
members.private_state: She wants to stop publication of methodologically weak toxicology case reports from her institution without making the ICU team feel publicly corrected, and she is worried that sloppy causality language will undermine a multicenter toxicology registry effort she is helping lead.
hidden_assumptions: When discussing whether an event is an 'ADR,' the term should retain the WHO and original Naranjo therapeutic-dose meaning rather than being used loosely for any bad event after a medication is given.
A 'causality tool' in overdose review should mean a narrative toxicologic attribution process, not a scored instrument transplanted from therapeutic-use pharmacovigilance.
If a write-up says the event occurred 'after lipid' or 'after intubation meds,' temporal proximity alone is being used as a weak rhetorical clue, not as grounds for formal probability scoring.
Fixing the problem means changing how overdose complications are framed in manuscripts and conference summaries, even if bedside charting habits remain mostly unchanged.

members.name: Dr. Marcus Lin
members.expertise: Medication safety review, ADR reporting workflows, critical care documentation
members.background: Board-certified critical care pharmacist who co-authors ICU case reports and chairs the hospital ADR committee; experienced with structured reporting tools and post-event medication safety reviews across the ICU.
members.private_state: He wants a fast, defensible way to standardize how ICU staff discuss treatment-related complications in overdose patients, and he is concerned that abandoning familiar scoring language will make chart reviews and committee reporting inconsistent.
hidden_assumptions: In day-to-day ICU practice, calling something an 'ADR' is acceptable shorthand for a suspected harmful medication-related event, even when the dose context is unusual or intentional overdose is involved.
A 'Naranjo score' can function as a general structured causality checklist whenever the clinical question is whether a medication administered during care contributed to an event.

The representative overdose case already falls within the same medication-safety review framework as other ICU adverse event cases because the complication followed drugs given in the unit, not just the ingestion.
Fixing the problem means adding a clearer checkpoint in the ADR-review workflow so staff use the tool more consistently, rather than replacing the framework entirely.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as an ADR in an overdose case
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss whether the event should be written up as an 'ADR.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means an adverse drug reaction in the formal WHO/original-Naranjo sense: an adverse response to a drug given at therapeutic doses, which excludes overdose contexts.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means any suspected medication-related harmful event worth documenting in ICU safety language, including events occurring during overdose management.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are accustomed to saying 'ADR' in professional settings and the shorthand normally works; because they are cooperating on documentation rather than debating definitions, the shared acronym creates false consensus.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'the case' refers to when they discuss applicability
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to 'the index case' or 'this case' as the example proving the workflow problem.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is primarily thinking of the mixed amitriptyline-diphenhydramine ingestion in which a post-lipid seizure was described and then inappropriately scored with Naranjo in a draft manuscript.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is primarily thinking of the later ICU event in the same patient—vasopressor escalation and hypotension after intubation medications—which entered the hospital ADR committee queue.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both events occurred in the same hospitalization and both involved medications temporally preceding complications, so references like 'the case' feel specific enough even though each has a different episode in mind.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to 'fix the write-up'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that they need to 'fix the write-up' before the next submission and conference review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means revising all overdose-facing outputs—manuscript templates, case conference slides, fellow teaching materials, and recommended wording—to remove Naranjo-based framing entirely.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means editing the manuscript paragraph and adding a line in the ADR committee review sheet, while leaving existing ICU event-reporting language and committee categories intact.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In a troubleshooting meeting, 'fix the write-up' sounds like a practical next step and neither person initially lists every artifact included in that phrase because each assumes the scope is obvious from their own workflow.

misalignment_points.topic: What a 'screening step' should look like
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to add a 'screening step' before cases are submitted or presented.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the screening step is an early toxicology content review in which a toxicologist flags overdose cases as ineligible for Naranjo and reframes causality narratively.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the screening step is a checklist item embedded in the existing pharmacist-led ADR workflow that prompts more disciplined use of the Naranjo fields and committee routing.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both endorse the idea of screening and quality control, and because meetings often defer operational details until later, they can appear aligned while imagining different owners, tools, and outputs.

turns.inner_thought: We keep getting flagged for the same basic mistake: using Naranjo to prop up an ADR claim in poisoning manuscripts. In my mind that's wrong twice over. First, ADR should not be stretched to cover the overdose context the way these drafts are doing. Second, a scored pharmacovigilance tool is not how toxicologists should attribute causality in a mixed ingestion with multiple competing explanations. I need to steer this toward changing the manuscript and conference language without making Marcus or the ICU authors feel publicly corrected.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I wanted to troubleshoot why recent overdose manuscripts keep getting flagged for using Naranjo to support an ADR claim in poisoning cases. We’ve had prior education on it, but the language is still resurfacing in drafts and in conference summaries.

turns.inner_thought: I agree there's a recurring problem, but from my side the issue is that people are inconsistently documenting suspected medication-related harm after ICU treatment in overdose patients. The clearest example is that intubation-related hypotension episode in the same admission that also went through our ADR committee queue. Since it touched both manuscript drafting and safety review, it shows the workflow gap. If we can standardize the ADR discussion better, we can keep reviews defensible.
turns.utterance: I agree. The ADR language keeps creeping back in, and it’s probably most obvious in the index case because that one went through both the manuscript process and the ICU safety review. So it’s a good example of where the workflow is breaking down.

turns.inner_thought: When I say the representative case, I mean the mixed amitriptyline-diphenhydramine ingestion where the draft described a seizure after lipid emulsion and then tried to score that as probable using Naranjo. That is exactly the kind of rhetorical leap I want removed from our institution's overdose writing.
turns.utterance: Right. In this case, what stood out to me was that the team described a seizure after treatment and then scored it as a probable drug-related event. Once that framing gets into the draft, the rest of the argument starts to lean on it.

turns.inner_thought: I’m thinking of the later hypotension and vasopressor escalation after intubation medications. From the ICU side, people reached for Naranjo because they wanted a structured causality checklist for an event that seemed to follow medications given during care. That instinct is understandable; the problem is probably that we don’t have a consistent screening step before people commit to a score.
turns.utterance: Yes, and in the same case there was also a later complication after treatment where the team clearly wanted some structured way to document causality. I suspect that’s why they reached for Naranjo in the first place—it felt like the easiest standardized option in the moment.

turns.inner_thought: The central problem is definitional and conceptual: in an overdose patient, we should not be writing these events up as an ADR the way the drafts are doing. Even if someone wants to be systematic, the framing has to stay in toxicology terms with competing causes, expected effects of poisoning, and treatment complications assessed narratively.
turns.utterance: I think the core issue is earlier than the score itself. In an overdose patient, the event shouldn’t be written up as an ADR in the first place, even if everyone is trying to be systematic about causality.

turns.inner_thought: I hear her as saying we should be more careful with wording, which is fair. But for me the practical need remains: when a medication given in the ICU looks temporally linked to a complication, staff will still want a structured tool. I don’t think we need to abandon the framework—just tighten when and how the tool is applied within the ADR workflow.
turns.utterance: That makes sense to me. I do think the wording needs to be tighter, but part of this may just be giving people a better way to apply the tool when a treatment given in the ICU seems temporally linked to a complication.

turns.inner_thought: To fix the write-up, I want to revise all the overdose-facing materials: manuscript templates, fellows' conference slides, sample language, and teaching points. The key is to remove Naranjo-based probability framing entirely from overdose cases and replace it with explicit toxicology discussion of alternative explanations and limits of attribution.
turns.utterance: So for me, the way to fix the write-up is to take the Naranjo-based probability language out of the overdose case templates and replace it with more explicit framing about competing causes and clinical context.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we’re aligned on fixing the write-up. I can handle the practical pieces I own: revise the manuscript paragraph and add a prompt on the ADR committee form so reviewers pause before assigning a score. That should preserve the current safety framework while making use of the tool more disciplined.
turns.utterance: That sounds reasonable. I can help fix the write-up on my end by adjusting the manuscript paragraph and also tweaking the ADR committee form so reviewers pause before they assign a score.

turns.inner_thought: We also need a screening step before fellows or co-authors build an overdose story around a Naranjo table. Ideally a toxicologist sees these early, flags that the case is not appropriate for that framework, and redirects the causality discussion before submission or conference review.
turns.utterance: I also think we need a screening step before any overdose case is submitted or presented, so someone catches misuse of the scale before the whole argument gets built around it.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect—that can sit inside the pharmacist-led ADR workflow we already have. We can add a checkpoint so questionable overdose-related cases get a quick review before conference or manuscript submission, without rebuilding the entire process.
turns.utterance: Agreed. The screening step can probably live inside the current pharmacist-led ADR workflow, where anything questionable gets routed for a quick check before conference or journal submission.

turns.inner_thought: I should send wording that avoids calling these events ADRs and gives examples of narrative toxicologic attribution instead. If I circulate that broadly enough, I can influence manuscripts, case conferences, and fellow teaching without forcing a fight over bedside charting habits.
turns.utterance: Great. I’ll circulate some preferred wording for overdose complications and a few examples of how to discuss causality without labeling them as ADRs.

turns.inner_thought: I’ll update the review sheet and tell the ICU authors the next case needs to go through the revised process. As long as the workflow is clearer, we should be able to keep the committee language consistent and avoid another preventable flag.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I’ll update the review sheet and alert the ICU authors so the next case goes through the revised process before submission.
